source_text: Diximus, quantum mediocritati nostrae licuit, de universis quae Baptismi religionem struunt; nunc ad reliquum statum ejus, aeque ut potero, progrediar de quaestiunculis quibusdam. Baptismus ab Joanne denuntiatus jam tunc habuit quaestionem ab ipso quidem Domino propositam Pharisaeis, coelestisne is Baptismus esset, an vero terrenus? De quo illi non valuerunt constanter respondere, utpote non intelligentes, quia non credentes. Nos porro quantula fide sumus, tantulo et intellectu possumus aestimare, divinum quidem eum Baptismum fuisse, mandatu tamen, non et potestate, quod et Joannem a Domino missum legimus in hoc munus caeterum humanum conditione. Nihil enim coeleste praestabat, sed coelestibus praeministrabat, poenitentiae scilicet praepositus, quae est in hominis potestate. Denique legis doctores et Pharisaei, qui credere noluerunt, nec poenitentiam egere. Quod si poenitentia humanum est, et Baptismus ipsius ejusdem conditionis fuerit necesse est; aut daret et Spiritum Sanctum et remissionem delictorum, si coelestis fuisset. Sed neque peccatum dimittit, neque Spiritum indulget, nisi Deus solus. Etiam ipse Dominus, nisi ipse prius ascenderet ad Patrem, aliter negavit, Spiritum descensurum. Id quod Dominus nondum conferebat, servus utique praestare non posset. Adeo postea in Actis apostolorum invenimus, quoniam qui Joannis Baptismum habebant, non accepissent Spiritum sanctum, quem ne auditu quidem noverant: ergo non erat coeleste, quod coelestia non exhibebat: cum ipsum quod coeleste in Joanne fuerat, spiritus prophetiae, post totius spiritus in Dominum translationem usque adeo defecerit, ut quem praedicaverat, quem advenientem designaverat, postmodum, an ipse esset miserit sciscitatum. Agebatur itaque Baptismus poenitentiae, quasi canditatus remissionis et sanctificationis in Christo subsecuturae. Nam quod praedicabat Baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem delictorum, in futuram remissionem enuntiatum est. Siquidem poenitentia antecedit, remissio subsequitur, et hoc est viam praeparare: qui autem praeparat, non idem ipse perficit, sed alii perficiendum procurat. Ipse profitetur sua non esse coelestia, sed Christi, dicendo: Qui de terra est, de terra loquitur: qui de supernis venit, super omnes est. Item, in sola poenitentia tinguere; venturum mox, qui tingueret in spiritu et igni. Scilicet, quia vera et stabilis aquae fides qua tinguitur in salutem; simulata autem et infirma, igni tinguitur in judicium.
pass_a_gloss: We said, as much as our mediocrity allowed, about all things which pertain to the religion of Baptism; now I will proceed, as much as I can, to the remaining state of it, about certain little questions. Baptism, announced by John, already had a question proposed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees, whether that Baptism was heavenly or truly earthly? About which those people were not able to respond constantly, as they were not understanding, because they were not believing. We, furthermore, with as much faith as we are, can also estimate with as much understanding, that that Baptism was indeed divine, but by command, not also by power, which we also read that John was sent by the Lord into this duty, nonetheless human in condition. For he was not exhibiting anything heavenly, but was serving heavenly things, namely, appointed over repentance, which is in human power. Finally, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, who did not want to believe, also did not undergo repentance. Which, if repentance is human, and the Baptism of it was of the same condition, it is necessary; or it would give both the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, if it were heavenly. But neither does it forgive sin, nor does it grant the Spirit, except God alone. Also, the Lord himself, unless he himself first ascended to the Father, otherwise denied that the Spirit would descend. What the Lord was not yet conferring, a servant certainly was not able to provide. So afterwards we find in the Acts of the Apostles, that those who had the Baptism of John had not received the Holy Spirit, whom they did not even know by hearing: therefore, it was not heavenly, because it was not exhibiting heavenly things: since the very thing that was heavenly in John, the spirit of prophecy, failed after the translation of the whole Spirit into the Lord, so much so that what he had predicted, what he had designated as coming, afterwards, he inquired whether he himself had sent. Therefore, the Baptism was being administered for repentance, as a candidate for the remission and sanctification in Christ that would follow. For what he was preaching, a Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, was announced for a future remission. Indeed, repentance precedes, remission follows, and this is to prepare the way: he who prepares, does not himself perfect, but procures for others to perfect. He himself confesses that his things are not heavenly, but Christ's, saying: He who is from the earth, speaks from the earth: he who comes from above, is above all. Also, to baptize only in repentance; soon to come, he who would baptize in Spirit and fire. Clearly, because the true and stable faith of water, by which one is baptized for salvation; but the simulated and weak, is baptized in fire for judgment.

pass_b_english: I have said as much as my limited ability allows about everything that constitutes the religion of Baptism; now I will move on, as best I can, to its remaining aspects, touching on a few minor questions. Baptism, announced by John, already faced a question posed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees: was that Baptism heavenly or earthly? They could not give a consistent answer, because they did not understand, because they did not believe. For our part, we can only gauge it with as much understanding as we have faith; we judge that Baptism was indeed divine, but by command, not by power. We read that John was sent by the Lord to that office, yet his condition remained human (John 3:31). He displayed nothing heavenly; rather, he served heavenly things, appointed to administer repentance, which lies within human power. Finally, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, who refused to believe, also refused to undergo repentance. If repentance is human, then the Baptism attached to it must share that same condition; otherwise, it would have conferred both the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, had it been heavenly. But it forgives no sin and grants no Spirit—God alone does that. Even the Lord himself declared that the Spirit would not descend unless he first ascended to the Father. What the Lord was not yet bestowing, a servant could certainly not supply. We see this confirmed afterward in the Acts of the Apostles: those who had received John's Baptism had not received the Holy Spirit; they had not even heard of him. Therefore, it was not heavenly, because it did not exhibit heavenly gifts. The very thing that was heavenly in John—the spirit of prophecy—failed completely after the full transfer of the Spirit to the Lord, so much so that John, who had predicted the Coming One and identified him, later sent to ask whether he himself was the one. Thus, the Baptism of repentance was administered as a candidate for the remission and sanctification in Christ that would follow. When he preached a Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, he announced a remission still future. Repentance precedes; remission follows. That is what it means to prepare the way: the one who prepares does not himself complete the work, but arranges for another to complete it. John himself confesses that his gifts are not heavenly, but Christ's, saying: "He who is from the earth speaks from the earth; he who comes from above is above all" (John 3:31). He baptized only in repentance; the One coming soon would baptize in Spirit and fire. Clearly, true and steadfast faith in the water brings baptism for salvation; counterfeit and weak faith brings baptism in fire for judgment (Acts 19:1-6).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the distinction between 'mandatu' (command) and 'potestate' (power), and the causal relationship regarding repentance and the Holy Spirit. Scripture citations in Pass B (John 3:31 and Acts 19:1-6) correctly identify the biblical loci alluded to in the Latin text. Pass A is a faithful literal gloss.
